questiontext.text:
Match the scientists listed in Column I with their corresponding contributions to the development of the periodic table in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Johann Dobereiner (i) Plotted physical properties like atomic volume against atomic weight
(B) John Alexander Newlands (ii) Observed regularities in X-ray spectra plotting \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against \(Z\)
(C) Lothar Meyer (iii) Formulated the Law of Triads based on atomic weight relationships
(D) Henry Moseley (iv) Proposed the Law of Octaves comparing elements to musical notes

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical contribution of Johann Dobereiner
In early 1800s, Johann Dobereiner observed that in certain groups of three elements (Triads), the middle element had an atomic weight approximately midway between the atomic weights of the other two members, and its chemical properties were intermediate.

Step 2: Historical contribution of John Alexander Newlands
In 1865, John Alexander Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of their atomic weights and found that every eighth element exhibited properties similar to the first element, resembling octaves in music (Law of Octaves).

Step 3: Historical contribution of Lothar Meyer
In 1869, Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties such as atomic volume, melting point, and boiling point against atomic weight, obtaining a periodically repeating curve with changing length of repeating patterns.

Step 4: Contribution of Henry Moseley
In 1913, Henry Moseley examined characteristic X-ray spectra across elements and established that a plot of \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against atomic number (\(Z\)) gives a straight line, proving that atomic number is the fundamental property governing periodicity.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Johann Dobereiner matches with Formulated the Law of Triads based on atomic weight relationships; John Alexander Newlands matches with Proposed the Law of Octaves comparing elements to musical notes; Lothar Meyer matches with Plotted physical properties like atomic volume against atomic weight; Henry Moseley matches with Observed regularities in X-ray spectra plotting \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against \(Z\).

questiontext.text:
Match the atomic numbers of elements listed in Column I with their corresponding IUPAC official names given in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) 104 (i) Copernicium
(B) 106 (ii) Rutherfordium
(C) 112 (iii) Oganesson
(D) 118 (iv) Seaborgium

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Element with atomic number 104
The element with atomic number 104 has the systematic IUPAC name Unnilquadium (symbol Unq) and its officially ratified IUPAC name is Rutherfordium (Rf).

Step 2: Element with atomic number 106
The element with atomic number 106 has the systematic IUPAC name Unnilhexium (symbol Unh) and was officially named Seaborgium (Sg) in honour of Glenn T. Seaborg.

Step 3: Element with atomic number 112
The element with atomic number 112 has the systematic IUPAC name Ununbium (symbol Uub) and its officially assigned IUPAC name is Copernicium (Cn).

Step 4: Element with atomic number 118
The element with atomic number 118 is a noble gas element with systematic IUPAC name Ununoctium (symbol Uuo) and official IUPAC name Oganesson (Og).

Therefore, the correct matching is: 104 matches with Rutherfordium; 106 matches with Seaborgium; 112 matches with Copernicium; 118 matches with Oganesson.

questiontext.text:
Match the items related to Mendeleev's periodic table in Column I with the corresponding descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Eka-Aluminium (i) Predicted element discovered later as Germanium with oxide \(\mathrm{EO_2}\)
(B) Eka-Silicon (ii) Lower atomic weight element placed after higher atomic weight element to maintain periodic family
(C) Tellurium and Iodine anomaly (iii) Oxide formula \(\mathrm{RO_3}\) representing the highest saline oxide
(D) Group VI elements in Mendeleev's table (iv) Predicted element discovered later as Gallium with oxide \(\mathrm{E_2O_3}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mendeleev's prediction for Eka-Aluminium
Mendeleev left a gap under aluminium and predicted an element termed Eka-Aluminium with an estimated atomic weight of 68 and oxide formula \(\mathrm{E_2O_3}\). This element was discovered later as Gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga_2O_3}\)).

Step 2: Mendeleev's prediction for Eka-Silicon
Mendeleev left a gap under silicon and predicted Eka-Silicon with an atomic weight of 72 and oxide formula \(\mathrm{EO_2}\). It was subsequently discovered as Germanium (\(\mathrm{GeO_2}\)).

Step 3: Tellurium and Iodine anomaly
Mendeleev placed iodine (atomic weight 126.9) in Group VII with the halogens after tellurium (atomic weight 127.6) in Group VI, disregarding strictly increasing atomic weights so that elements with similar properties remained in the same vertical column.

Step 4: Group VI higher oxide formula
In Mendeleev's published periodic system, elements belonging to Group VI have the characteristic highest saline oxide formula of \(\mathrm{RO_3}\) (such as \(\mathrm{SO_3}\), \(\mathrm{SeO_3}\), \(\mathrm{TeO_3}\)).

Therefore, the correct matching is: Eka-Aluminium matches with Predicted element discovered later as Gallium with oxide \(\mathrm{E_2O_3}\); Eka-Silicon matches with Predicted element discovered later as Germanium with oxide \(\mathrm{EO_2}\); Tellurium and Iodine anomaly matches with Lower atomic weight element placed after higher atomic weight element to maintain periodic family; Group VI elements in Mendeleev's table matches with Oxide formula \(\mathrm{RO_3}\) representing the highest saline oxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q04 - Periodic table blocks and electron configurations

questiontext.text:
Match the block/category of elements in Column I with their general outer electronic configurations in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) s-Block elements (i) \(\mathrm{(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}}\)
(B) p-Block elements (ii) \(\mathrm{ns^{1-2}}\)
(C) d-Block elements (iii) \(\mathrm{(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2}\)
(D) f-Block elements (iv) \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^{1-6}}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Outer electronic configuration of s-block elements
Elements of Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 2 (alkaline earth metals) have valence configurations of \(\mathrm{ns^1}\) and \(\mathrm{ns^2}\) respectively, yielding the general outer configuration \(\mathrm{ns^{1-2}}\).

Step 2: Outer electronic configuration of p-block elements
Elements of Groups 13 to 18 possess outer electronic configurations varying across periods from \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^1}\) to \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^6}\).

Step 3: Outer electronic configuration of d-block elements
Transition elements (Groups 3 to 12) involve the progressive filling of penultimate d-orbitals and possess the general outer configuration \(\mathrm{(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}}\) (for instance, Pd has \(\mathrm{4d^{10}5s^0}\)).

Step 4: Outer electronic configuration of f-block elements
Inner-transition elements comprising the lanthanoids and actinoids are characterized by the progressive filling of antipenultimate f-orbitals with the general outer configuration \(\mathrm{(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2}\).

Therefore, the correct matching is: s-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{ns^{1-2}}\); p-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^{1-6}}\); d-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}}\); f-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2}\).

questiontext.text:
Match the groups/blocks of elements in Column I with their prominent chemical and physical features in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Group 1 (Alkali metals) (i) Possess large negative electron gain enthalpies and readily accept electrons
(B) Group 16 (Chalcogens) (ii) Exhibit variable oxidation states, coloured ions, and catalytic activity
(C) Groups 3 to 12 (Transition metals) (iii) Highly reactive metals with low ionization enthalpies forming \(1+\) ions
(D) Actinoids (iv) Radioactive series displaying a wide range of oxidation states due to small energy differences

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Properties of Group 1 elements
Alkali metals have low ionization enthalpies, lose their single valence electron readily to form \(1+\) cations, and are highly electropositive and reactive, forming predominantly ionic compounds.

Step 2: Properties of Group 16 elements
Chalcogens require two electrons to attain a stable octet noble gas configuration; they exhibit highly negative electron gain enthalpies and pronounced non-metallic character.

Step 3: Properties of Groups 3 to 12 elements
Transition metals are characterized by partially filled d-orbitals, variable oxidation states, coloured hydrated ions or complexes, paramagnetism, and frequent use as catalysts.

Step 4: Properties of Actinoids
Actinoids are radioactive elements where early members exhibit complicated chemistry with multiple oxidation states because 5f, 6d, and 7s energy levels are comparable in energy.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Group 1 (Alkali metals) matches with Highly reactive metals with low ionization enthalpies forming \(1+\) ions; Group 16 (Chalcogens) matches with Possess large negative electron gain enthalpies and readily accept electrons; Groups 3 to 12 (Transition metals) matches with Exhibit variable oxidation states, coloured ions, and catalytic activity; Actinoids matches with Radioactive series displaying a wide range of oxidation states due to small energy differences.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q06 - Anomalous behavior of second period elements

questiontext.text:
Match each anomalous property/behavior of second-period elements in Column I with its underlying scientific rationale in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Boron forms only \(\mathrm{[BF_4]^-}\) whereas aluminium forms \(\mathrm{[AlF_6]^{3-}}\) (i) Similarity in ionic potential (charge-to-radius ratio) and electronegativity
(B) Carbon and nitrogen readily form stable multiple bonds to themselves (ii) Small atomic size enabling effective sideways overlap of unhybridized \(2p\) orbitals
(C) Lithium and beryllium form compounds with pronounced covalent character (iii) Absence of \(d\)-orbitals restricting the maximum covalency to four
(D) Diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium (iv) Extremely small cation size resulting in exceptionally high polarising power

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Covalency limitation of boron
The second-period elements have only four valence orbitals (one \(2s\) and three \(2p\)) and lack \(d\)-orbitals. Therefore, the maximum covalency of boron is strictly four (as in \(\mathrm{[BF_4]^-}\)), while aluminium can expand its octet to six using vacant \(3d\) orbitals to form \(\mathrm{[AlF_6]^{3-}}\).

Step 2: Multiple bonding in second-period elements
Carbon and nitrogen have compact atomic radii, which allows their \(2p\) atomic orbitals to approach closely and form strong \(p_\pi - p_\pi\) multiple bonds with themselves and each other (e.g., \(\mathrm{C=C}\), \(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\), \(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\)).

Step 3: Covalent nature of lithium and beryllium compounds
Due to their very small ionic radii, \(\mathrm{Li^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Be^{2+}}\) have exceptionally high charge/radius ratios (polarising power), which polarises anions significantly and introduces substantial covalent character according to Fajan's rules.

Step 4: Diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium
Beryllium and aluminium resemble each other diagonally across the periodic table because the increase in size going down is compensated by the increase in charge and reduction in size going across, leading to similar charge-to-radius ratios and electronegativities.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Boron forms only \(\mathrm{[BF_4]^-}\) whereas aluminium forms \(\mathrm{[AlF_6]^{3-}}\) matches with Absence of \(d\)-orbitals restricting the maximum covalency to four; Carbon and nitrogen readily form stable multiple bonds to themselves matches with Small atomic size enabling effective sideways overlap of unhybridized \(2p\) orbitals; Lithium and beryllium form compounds with pronounced covalent character matches with Extremely small cation size resulting in exceptionally high polarising power; Diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium matches with Similarity in ionic potential (charge-to-radius ratio) and electronegativity.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q07 - Periodic trends in oxide acidity and basicity

questiontext.text:
Match the oxides listed in Column I with their correct chemical behavior in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) (i) Strongly acidic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) upon dissolution in water
(B) \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) (ii) Strongly basic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) upon reaction with water
(C) \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\) (iii) Neutral oxide that exhibits neither acidic nor basic properties
(D) \(\mathrm{CO}\) (iv) Amphoteric oxide that reacts with both strong acids and strong bases

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\)
Sodium is an electropositive alkali metal on the extreme left of the third period. Its normal oxide, \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\), reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{Na_2O + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH}\)), demonstrating strong basicity.

Step 2: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)
Aluminium lies in the center of the third period. Its oxide, \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), is amphoteric; it dissolves in both acidic and basic solutions, forming aluminium salts and aluminate species respectively.

Step 3: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\)
Chlorine is an electronegative non-metal on the extreme right of the period. Its highest oxide, \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\), dissolves in water to form the strong acid perchloric acid (\(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HClO_4}\)), demonstrating strongly acidic nature.

Step 4: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{CO}\)
Carbon monoxide (\(\mathrm{CO}\)), along with \(\mathrm{NO}\) and \(\mathrm{N_2O}\), does not form salts with either acids or bases, classifying it as a neutral oxide.

Therefore, the correct matching is: \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) matches with Strongly basic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) upon reaction with water; \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) matches with Amphoteric oxide that reacts with both strong acids and strong bases; \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\) matches with Strongly acidic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) upon dissolution in water; \(\mathrm{CO}\) matches with Neutral oxide that exhibits neither acidic nor basic properties.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q08 - Explanations for first ionization enthalpy anomalies

questiontext.text:
Match the comparative ionization enthalpy trends in Column I with the dominant governing factors responsible for them in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Boron has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Beryllium (i) Pairing of two electrons in the same \(2p\) orbital creates enhanced interelectronic repulsion
(B) Oxygen has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Nitrogen (ii) Single valence electron is located in a distant \(ns\) orbital well shielded by noble gas core
(C) Noble gases exhibit peak ionization enthalpies in each period (iii) Completely filled, closed valence shells possessing exceptionally high electronic stability
(D) Alkali metals display lowest first ionization enthalpies in each period (iv) Outermost electron resides in a \(2p\) orbital which is more shielded and less penetrating than a \(2s\) orbital

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: First ionization enthalpy difference between Boron and Beryllium
In beryllium (\(1s^2 2s^2\)), an electron is removed from a penetrating, fully filled \(2s\) subshell. In boron (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\)), the electron is removed from a \(2p\) subshell, which experiences greater shielding from the core \(1s\) and inner \(2s\) electrons and penetrates less toward the nucleus, making it easier to detach.

Step 2: First ionization enthalpy difference between Oxygen and Nitrogen
Nitrogen has an electronic configuration of \(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\), an extra-stable half-filled \(p\) subshell. Oxygen (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\)) contains two paired electrons in one of the \(2p\) orbitals. Mutual repulsion between these paired electrons facilitates the removal of the fourth \(2p\) electron.

Step 3: Exceptionally high ionization enthalpies of noble gases
Noble gases have completely filled valence shells (\(ns^2 np^6\), or \(1s^2\) for He). This closed electronic shell has maximum stability and large effective nuclear charge, requiring tremendous energy to remove an electron.

Step 4: Minimum ionization enthalpies of alkali metals
Alkali metals have a single valence \(ns^1\) electron situated outside a stable noble gas core. Because inner complete shells effectively screen the nuclear charge, this electron is held loosely and is detached with minimal energy.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Boron has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Beryllium matches with Outermost electron resides in a \(2p\) orbital which is more shielded and less penetrating than a \(2s\) orbital; Oxygen has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Nitrogen matches with Pairing of two electrons in the same \(2p\) orbital creates enhanced interelectronic repulsion; Noble gases exhibit peak ionization enthalpies in each period matches with Completely filled, closed valence shells possessing exceptionally high electronic stability; Alkali metals display lowest first ionization enthalpies in each period matches with Single valence electron is located in a distant \(ns\) orbital well shielded by noble gas core.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q09 - Periodic trends in electron gain enthalpy

questiontext.text:
Match the observations on electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{eg}H\)) in Column I with the corresponding scientific explanations in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Chlorine has a more negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than fluorine (i) Added electron must occupy an orbital in the next principal shell, yielding an unstable state
(B) Noble gases have positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) values (ii) Added electron enters a larger \(3p\) region of space with significantly lower electron repulsion
(C) Group 17 halogens have the highest negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (iii) Compact \(2p\) subshell results in strong repulsion that reduces enthalpy released compared to sulphur
(D) Oxygen has a less negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than sulphur (iv) High effective nuclear charge allows acquisition of a stable octet by adding a single electron

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reason for \(\Delta_{eg}H\) difference between chlorine and fluorine
In fluorine (\(n = 2\)), the incoming electron enters a very compact \(2p\) subshell and suffers substantial interelectronic repulsion. In chlorine (\(n = 3\)), the electron enters a more spacious \(3p\) orbital with much lower electron-electron repulsion, resulting in more heat released (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for Cl versus \(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for F).

Step 2: Reason for positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) of noble gases
Noble gas atoms have completely filled valence shells. An extra electron cannot be accommodated in the existing valence shell and must enter the next higher principal quantum shell, which requires energy input (endothermic process, positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\)).

Step 3: Reason for highly negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) of halogens
Halogens have a \(ns^2 np^5\) configuration with only one electron deficient from a stable octet and possess high effective nuclear charges across their periods, giving them a very strong tendency to gain an electron.

Step 4: Reason for \(\Delta_{eg}H\) difference between oxygen and sulphur
Similar to fluorine, oxygen has a very small atomic size (\(n = 2\)). The incoming electron added to oxygen experiences significant electron-electron repulsion, making its \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (\(-141\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) less negative than that of sulphur (\(-200\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Therefore, the correct matching is: Chlorine has a more negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than fluorine matches with Added electron enters a larger \(3p\) region of space with significantly lower electron repulsion; Noble gases have positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) values matches with Added electron must occupy an orbital in the next principal shell, yielding an unstable state; Group 17 halogens have the highest negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) matches with High effective nuclear charge allows acquisition of a stable octet by adding a single electron; Oxygen has a less negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than sulphur matches with Compact \(2p\) subshell results in strong repulsion that reduces enthalpy released compared to sulphur.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q10 - Element reactivity from ionization enthalpy data

questiontext.text:
The first ionization enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H_1\)), second ionization enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H_2\)), and electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{eg}H\)) in \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) of four elements W, X, Y, and Z are provided below:

Element \(\Delta_i H_1\) \(\Delta_i H_2\) \(\Delta_{eg}H\)
W 2372 5251 +48
X 419 3051 -48
Y 1681 3374 -328
Z 520 7300 -60

Match the elements in Column I with their corresponding chemical descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Element W (i) Most reactive non-metal (Halogen)
(B) Element X (ii) Most reactive metal exhibiting the lowest \(\Delta_i H_1\)
(C) Element Y (iii) Least reactive element with noble gas electronic configuration
(D) Element Z (iv) Alkali metal forming predominantly covalent halides due to small size

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Element W
Element W exhibits an exceptionally high first ionization enthalpy (\(2372\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and a positive electron gain enthalpy (\(+48\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). This demonstrates a completely filled, closed electronic shell characteristic of noble gases (specifically Helium), making it the least reactive element.

Step 2: Evaluation of Element X
Element X has the lowest first ionization enthalpy among the metals listed (\(419\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and a moderately large second ionization enthalpy (\(3051\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). This corresponds to Potassium, an alkali metal with the highest metallic reactivity.

Step 3: Evaluation of Element Y
Element Y possesses a very high first ionization enthalpy (\(1681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) together with a strongly negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). These values indicate a halogen atom (specifically Fluorine), which is the most reactive non-metal.

Step 4: Evaluation of Element Z
Element Z has a first ionization enthalpy of \(520\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) followed by an immense jump in its second ionization enthalpy to \(7300\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). This indicates a single valence electron outside a closed shell with very small ionic size (corresponding to Lithium). Due to the high polarising power of its cation, it forms halides with pronounced covalent character.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Element W matches with Least reactive element with noble gas electronic configuration; Element X matches with Most reactive metal exhibiting the lowest \(\Delta_i H_1\); Element Y matches with Most reactive non-metal (Halogen); Element Z matches with Alkali metal forming predominantly covalent halides due to small size.
